newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Politics the stumbling block to New Zealand easing.
newsitem.headline: Politics the stumbling block to New Zealand easing.

text.p: New Zealand's failure to form a government since the October 12 election is the only excuse the central bank has left not to sanction a fall in interest rates, economists and traders said on Tuesday.

They were commenting on figures showing ordinary time wages rose 3.4 percent in the August year, in line with forecasts, but the more important private sector earnings rose only 3.7 percent against forecasts of 4.2 percent.
Economists said the data showed that inflationary pressures in the labour market had peaked, paving the way for an easing in monetary policy over the next six months.

The only thing holding the central bank back now was the failure of political parties to form a government and worries that the projected budget surplus will be blown away by parties competing to win power, they said.
"It leaves the one outstanding item on the agenda as fiscal policy," said Bankers Trust Executive Vice President John McFarlane.

The nationalist New Zealand First party holds the balance of power and for five weeks has been in coalition talks with the conservative National caretaker government and the left-of-centre Labour Party.

Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash is so concerned about talk of new government spending, which is putting upward pressure on interest rates and the dollar, that he told politicians last week that they may need to defer the second half of a NZ$3 billion tax cut package due next year.
While the spending risk remains, economists said Tuesday's figures were reassuring for the Reserve Bank after earlier data showing house prices easing and full-time job growth static.

"This number goes pretty close to eliminating the wages risk. It certainly makes it less of a problem. It's difficult to say, as yet, whether it means there is going to be an easing," said Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek.
The Reserve Bank has been grappling for six quarters with inflation at the top of, or above, the bank's 0-2 percent inflation target.
Last month, after much better than expected September quarter inflation data, it said it needed more evidence of inflation pressures abating before it eased.
"All the partial indicators that we have had through so far are very positive in terms of the outlook for inflation over the next six to nine months," said Westpac economist Hamish Macalister.
In the debt market, 10 year bonds rallied five basis points to 7.18 percent and traders suggested they could rally down to the bottom of their recent range at around 7.0 percent.
The indicator 90-day bank bill yields fell just three points to 8.95 percent.
"Generally we would expect the market to trade reasonably positively on the numbers," said National Bank's joint head of treasury Simon Tyler.
"Of more influence on the market will be the political situation. The economic data suggests things are on track, but potentially there are some policy changes in store."
He cited a likely change to the Reserve Bank's inflation target, substantial spending initiatives and the possible deferral of the second round of the tax cut package next year as on the agenda.
